questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A fern produces two visibly different spore sizes, and the large spore develops into a female gametophyte. Which inference is warranted?
options: A) All fern spores are diploid
B) This fern is heterosporous, with megaspores giving female gametophytes
C) The small spores become sporophytes directly
D) The large spores are seeds enclosed by fruit
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) This fern is heterosporous, with megaspores giving female gametophytes.
Why: Most pteridophytes make spores of one kind (homosporous). A few, such as Selaginella and Salvinia, make two kinds: small microspores and large megaspores. The megaspore grows into a female gametophyte and the microspore into a male gametophyte. The female gametophyte is kept on the parent plant for some time, which is seen as a step towards the seed habit.
Why not the others: (A) Spores are formed by meiosis and are haploid. (C) A spore grows into a gametophyte, never directly into a sporophyte. (D) Pteridophytes have no seeds or fruits.
Key point: Heterospory: microspore → male, megaspore → female gametophyte.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The labelled frog heart has two atria draining into one ventricle. Which chamber directly receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Left atrium.
Why: The frog's heart has three chambers: two atria and one ventricle. Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. Deoxygenated blood from the body collects in the sinus venosus and enters the right atrium. Both atria open into the single ventricle, where the two kinds of blood mix.
Why not the others: (A) The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body. (B) The ventricle receives blood from the atria, not directly from the lungs. (D) The sinus venosus receives blood from the venae cavae and opens into the right atrium.
Key point: Lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium, in the frog as in humans.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two equal cells are placed in the same hypertonic solution. Cell X loses water and shrinks; cell Y initially shrinks but then returns toward its original volume when a specific solute carrier is activated. Which control most directly tests whether carrier-dependent solute uptake drives Y's recovery?
options: A) Block the carrier in Y while holding external osmolarity fixed
B) Remove X from the experiment
C) Change both solution osmolarities unpredictably
D) Increase light intensity without monitoring solute
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Block the carrier in Y while holding external osmolarity fixed.
Why: To test whether the carrier causes the recovery, the carrier must be the only thing changed. If Y fails to recover when the carrier is blocked, with everything else the same, the recovery depended on solute uptake through that carrier: solute enters, the cell's solute concentration rises and water follows by osmosis.
Why not the others: (B) Removing X takes away the comparison without testing the carrier. (C) Changing the solutions unpredictably adds new variables. (D) Light has nothing to do with the proposed mechanism, and solute would not even be measured.
Key point: Change one factor and keep the rest constant.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The leaf section shows a ring of chloroplast-rich bundle-sheath cells around each vascular bundle and an outer mesophyll layer. Which interpretation fits this anatomy and its carbon-fixation role?
options: A) Kranz anatomy supports C4 transfer of four-carbon acids to bundle-sheath Calvin-cycle cells
B) It proves photorespiration is impossible at all temperatures
C) It is a nonphotosynthetic stem cross-section
D) It is ordinary C3 anatomy with no bundle-sheath function
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Kranz anatomy supports C4 transfer of four-carbon acids to bundle-sheath Calvin-cycle cells.
Why: A wreath of large bundle-sheath cells packed with chloroplasts around each vascular bundle is Kranz anatomy, the mark of a C₄ leaf. CO₂ is first fixed in the mesophyll by PEP carboxylase into a four-carbon acid. The acid moves to the bundle-sheath cells and releases CO₂ there, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle operate.
Why not the others: (B) Photorespiration is greatly reduced in C₄ plants, but anatomy alone does not prove it impossible. (C) Vascular bundles ringed by green cells and mesophyll describe a leaf, not a stem. (D) In C₃ leaves the bundle-sheath cells are not specialised in this way.
Key point: Kranz anatomy = C₄; mesophyll fixes, bundle sheath runs the Calvin cycle.
questions.image_alt: A leaf vascular bundle is surrounded by bundle sheath and mesophyll.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A healthy adult has a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. What is the pulse pressure, and during which event of the cardiac cycle is the higher value recorded?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 40 mm Hg; ventricular systole.
Given: Blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg: systolic 120, diastolic 80.
Formula/Principle: Pulse pressure = systolic pressure − diastolic pressure.
Step 1: Pulse pressure = 120 − 80 = 40 mm Hg.
Step 2: The higher value is the pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract and force blood into them.
Step 3: The lower value is the arterial pressure when the ventricles relax.
Why: Arterial pressure rises and falls with each heartbeat. Contraction of the ventricles (systole) pushes blood into the aorta and gives the peak of 120 mm Hg. During relaxation (diastole) the elastic arteries keep the pressure from falling below about 80 mm Hg.
Why not the others: (A) 200 is the sum of the two readings, and the atria do not produce arterial pressure. (B) 100 is their average, and diastole gives the lower reading. (D) The value 40 is right, but the higher reading belongs to systole.
Key point: 120 = systolic, 80 = diastolic; difference = pulse pressure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A human primary spermatocyte completes meiosis normally. How many functional haploid sperm can ultimately arise from it, assuming all products survive maturation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Four.
Why: A primary spermatocyte is diploid. Meiosis I gives two haploid secondary spermatocytes, and meiosis II gives four haploid spermatids. Each spermatid changes into a sperm (spermiogenesis), so one primary spermatocyte gives four sperm.
Why not the others: (A) One functional gamete from a meiosis is the case in the female, where three polar bodies are lost. (B) Two is the number of cells after meiosis I only. (C) Three is the number of polar bodies in oogenesis.
Key point: Spermatogenesis: 1 → 4 sperm. Oogenesis: 1 → 1 ovum.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two unlinked loci segregate independently in an AaBb × AaBb cross, with complete dominance at each locus. Given that an offspring shows a dominant phenotype at at least one locus, what is the probability it is homozygous recessive at exactly one locus?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/5.
Given: AaBb × AaBb, unlinked, complete dominance. Phenotype classes out of 16: A_B_ 9, A_bb 3, aaB_ 3, aabb 1.
Formula/Principle: P(X | Y) = n(X and Y) ÷ n(Y).
Step 1: Dominant phenotype at one locus or both: 9 + 3 + 3 = 15.
Step 2: Homozygous recessive at exactly one locus: A_bb (3) and aaB_ (3) = 6; all of these are among the 15.
Step 3: P = 6/15 = 2/5.
Why: The condition removes only the aabb class. Within what remains, the offspring that are recessive at exactly one locus are the two single-dominant classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
Why not the others: (B) 3/8 is 6/16, without applying the condition. (C) 1/4 is the chance of being recessive at one named locus. (D) 1/2 has no basis in the ratio.
Key point: Use the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 classes and reduce the sample space.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A tumour sample has a mutation disabling a cell-cycle checkpoint that normally responds to DNA damage. Which pattern is most consistent with loss of that checkpoint?
options: A) More time for DNA repair before mitosis
B) Cells enter division despite unrepaired lesions
C) No further DNA replication in any cells
D) All cells immediately undergo normal differentiation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cells enter division despite unrepaired lesions.
Why: Checkpoints stop the cell cycle when DNA is damaged, which gives time for repair or sends the cell to its death. If the checkpoint does not work, damaged cells go on to replicate and divide, mutations build up and growth is no longer controlled. This is a common step in the development of cancer.
Why not the others: (A) A working checkpoint provides time for repair; losing it removes that time. (C) Without the checkpoint, replication continues unchecked. (D) Tumour cells typically fail to differentiate normally.
Key point: Lost checkpoint → division with damaged DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A proposed gene-edited crop resists a fungal infection in greenhouse tests. Which observation most directly tests whether the edit, rather than background variation, caused resistance?
options: A) Only compare edited plants after spraying different doses
B) Measure leaf colour in one edited plant
C) Compare independently edited lines with isogenic unedited controls under the same inoculum
D) Assume a marker band proves field resistance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Compare independently edited lines with isogenic unedited controls under the same inoculum.
Why: Isogenic controls have the same genetic background and differ only in the edit, so any difference in resistance can be traced to the edit. Several independently edited lines guard against a chance change elsewhere in one line. Using the same amount of fungus on all plants removes differences in exposure.
Why not the others: (A) Without unedited plants there is nothing to compare with, and the doses differ too. (B) Leaf colour in one plant measures neither resistance nor repeatability. (D) A marker band shows that the DNA is present, not that the plant resists disease.
Key point: Same background, same treatment, one difference, several replicates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A protected forest and a similarly sized unprotected forest are surveyed for species with equal effort. The protected site has more species now, but it already had more before protection. Which added comparison best tests conservation effect?
options: B) Species names in a single plot
D) Change in each site's species count from before to after protection
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Change in each site's species count from before to after protection.
Why: The protected site was richer even before protection, so its present lead may only reflect that starting difference. Comparing how much each site changed over the same period separates the effect of protection from the starting difference; the unprotected site shows what would have happened anyway.
Why not the others: (A) Present totals cannot be separated from the initial difference. (B) Names from a single plot do not measure richness over the site. (C) The sites are similar in size, so area tells nothing new.
Key point: Compare changes over time, with a control site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An X-linked recessive disorder affects a boy, while his father is unaffected. His mother is unaffected and has one affected brother. Assuming no new mutations, what is the probability that the mother's next son is affected, given she is confirmed a carrier by the affected boy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: X-linked recessive disorder; affected boy; unaffected father; unaffected mother, now known to be a carrier (XᴬXᵃ).
Formula/Principle: A son receives his X chromosome from his mother and his Y chromosome from his father.
Step 1: The mother's eggs carry Xᴬ or Xᵃ with probability 1/2 each.
Step 2: A son is XᴬY (unaffected) or XᵃY (affected), depending only on the egg.
Step 3: P(next son affected) = 1/2.
Why: The affected boy must have received Xᵃ from his mother, since his father gave him a Y. This fixes the mother as a carrier. Her affected brother agrees with this but adds nothing more once she is known to be a carrier, and each birth is an independent event.
Why not the others: (A) 1/4 is the chance that any child is an affected son, counting daughters too; the question asks about a son. (C) 1/3 has no basis here. (D) 1 would need the mother to be homozygous for the allele, and then she would be affected herself.
Key point: Carrier mother: half her sons are affected.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At a synapse, excitatory transmitter release and receptor binding are normal, but a second inhibitory input arrives simultaneously. The recorded membrane potential rises by 4 mV with excitation alone and by only 1 mV when both inputs fire. What inference is strongest?
options: A) Excitatory vesicle fusion was abolished
B) The inhibitory input must be located in the presynaptic cell
C) Postsynaptic summation reduced net depolarisation
D) All receptors became permanently inactive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Postsynaptic summation reduced net depolarisation.
Why: A neuron adds up the excitatory and inhibitory potentials that reach it at the same time. Excitation alone gives +4 mV. With the inhibitory input the result is only +1 mV, so the inhibitory input contributes about −3 mV. The stem states that excitatory release and binding are normal.
Why not the others: (A) Excitatory release is stated to be normal. (B) The recording shows the combined effect on the postsynaptic membrane; it does not locate the inhibition in the presynaptic cell. (D) The cell still depolarises by 1 mV, and excitation alone still works.
Key point: Net potential = sum of excitatory and inhibitory potentials.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, blood glucose rises in a healthy person. Which paired endocrine response is expected to move glucose toward baseline?
options: B) Insulin rises, glucagon also rises to the same effect
D) Insulin rises and glucagon falls
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Insulin rises and glucagon falls.
Why: A rise in blood glucose stimulates the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans to secrete insulin, which makes liver, muscle and fat cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen. At the same time the α-cells secrete less glucagon, the hormone that raises blood glucose by breaking down glycogen.
Why not the others: (A) Less insulin and more glucagon would raise blood glucose further. (B) The two hormones have opposite effects. (C) Both hormones are always present; only their amounts change.
Key point: Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A plant-cell homogenate yields a low-speed nuclear pellet, then a fraction rich in chlorophyll and thylakoid membranes. Which process is best enriched in the second fraction under illumination?
options: A) Light-driven electron transport and proton-gradient formation
D) Protein translation solely on free cytosolic ribosomes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Light-driven electron transport and proton-gradient formation.
Why: A fraction rich in chlorophyll and thylakoid membranes consists of chloroplasts or their membranes. The thylakoid membranes hold the photosystems and electron carriers. In light they pass electrons from water to NADP⁺ and pump protons into the lumen, and this gradient drives ATP synthesis.
Why not the others: (B) Nuclear DNA is in the first, low-speed pellet. (C) Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol, which stays in the supernatant. (D) Free ribosomes are much smaller and remain in the supernatant.
Key point: Thylakoid membranes: light reactions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In humans, where does fertilisation normally take place, and at what stage does the embryo become implanted in the uterine wall?
options: A) In the uterus; as a zygote
B) In the ampullary region of the fallopian tube; as a blastocyst
C) In the ovary; as a morula
D) In the cervix; as a gastrula
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) In the ampullary region of the fallopian tube; as a blastocyst.
Why: The ovum released from the ovary is picked up by the fimbriae and meets the sperm in the ampulla, the wide part of the fallopian tube. The zygote divides as it moves towards the uterus, passing through the morula stage, and reaches it as a blastocyst. The blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium; this is implantation.
Why not the others: (A) Fertilisation does not occur in the uterus, and the embryo has divided many times before it implants. (C) The ovum is fertilised after it leaves the ovary, and the morula changes into a blastocyst before implantation. (D) The cervix is the neck of the uterus; the gastrula forms after implantation.
Key point: Fertilisation: ampulla. Implantation: blastocyst.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which of the following molecules has an odd number of electrons, so that not all its atoms can have a complete octet?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) NO.
Why: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and oxygen 6, so NO has 11. With an odd number, the electrons cannot all be paired, and one atom is left with fewer than eight. Such odd-electron molecules, NO and NO₂ among them, are exceptions to the octet rule.
Why not the others: (A) N₂ has 10 valence electrons and a triple bond; each atom has an octet. (C) CO₂ has 16 valence electrons, all paired. (D) H₂O has 8 valence electrons; oxygen has an octet and each hydrogen a duplet.
Key point: Octet exceptions: odd-electron molecules, incomplete octets, expanded octets.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ambidentate donor connectivity and linkage isomerism
questions.question: The two structures have identical composition \([\ce{Co(NH3)5(NO2)}]\ce{Cl2}\). In X the metal is bonded to nitrogen of the NO₂ ligand; in Y it is bonded to oxygen of that ligand. What kind of isomerism distinguishes them, and what is the coordination number in each?
options: B) Ionisation; six in X and five in Y
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Linkage; six in each.
Why: NO₂⁻ is an ambidentate ligand: it can bind through nitrogen (nitro, –NO₂) or through oxygen (nitrito, –ONO). Two complexes that differ only in which atom of the ligand is bonded to the metal are linkage isomers. In both, cobalt is bonded to five nitrogen atoms of ammonia and one atom of the NO₂ group, so the coordination number is six.
Why not the others: (A) Geometrical isomers differ in the positions of ligands, not in the donor atom, and the coordination number is not five. (B) Ionisation isomers exchange a ligand with a counter-ion; here both have two chloride counter-ions. (D) Neither complex is chiral, and cobalt does not have seven donor atoms.
Key point: Ambidentate ligand (NO₂⁻, SCN⁻) → linkage isomerism.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: What is the maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have the quantum numbers n = 4 and l = 2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10.
Given: n = 4, l = 2.
Formula/Principle: For a given l, m_l takes the 2l + 1 values −l … +l; each orbital holds 2 electrons.
Step 1: l = 2 is a d subshell, so n = 4, l = 2 is the 4d subshell.
Step 2: Number of orbitals = 2l + 1 = 5 (m_l = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2).
Worked derivation: \[\text{maximum electrons}=2(2l+1)=2\times5=10\]
Why: Each orbital is fixed by n, l and m_l. By the Pauli principle it can hold two electrons with opposite spins. A subshell therefore holds 2(2l + 1) electrons: 2 for s, 6 for p, 10 for d and 14 for f.
Why not the others: (A) 2 is the capacity of one orbital, or of an s subshell. (B) 5 is the number of orbitals, not of electrons. (C) 6 is the capacity of a p subshell.
Key point: Subshell capacity = 2(2l + 1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: A molecule contains both a nonconjugated C=C double bond and a ketone C=O group. One equivalent of Br₂ is added in dry CCl₄ in the dark. Which electron-pair movement starts the characteristic bromine addition, and what group remains unchanged at this stage?
options: A) The alkene π pair attacks electrophilic Br; the ketone C=O remains
B) Carbonyl oxygen attacks Br⁻; the alkene remains
C) The ketone π pair attacks Br⁻; the alkene remains
D) The alkene π pair attacks Br⁻; the carbonyl oxygen leaves
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The alkene π pair attacks electrophilic Br; the ketone C=O remains.
Why: The π electrons of a C=C bond are loosely held and act as a nucleophile. As a bromine molecule approaches, it is polarised and its nearer atom becomes the electrophile; the π pair attacks it and a bromide ion is released. The ion then adds to give the dibromide. The carbonyl carbon is itself electron-poor and does not react with an electrophile such as bromine under these conditions.
Why not the others: (B) Bromide ion is a nucleophile; an oxygen lone pair does not attack it. (C) The C=O π bond is polarised towards oxygen and is not attacked by bromine in this way. (D) The alkene attacks the electrophilic bromine atom, not the bromide ion, and oxygen does not leave.
Key point: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; carbonyl groups undergo nucleophilic addition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Ethene is bubbled through cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄ solution. What is observed, and what organic product is formed?
options: A) The purple colour is discharged; ethane-1,2-diol is formed
B) The purple colour is discharged; ethane is formed
C) No change occurs; ethene does not react
D) The solution turns orange; 1,2-dibromoethane is formed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The purple colour is discharged; ethane-1,2-diol is formed.
Why: Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) oxidises the C=C bond of an alkene, adding an –OH group to each carbon to give a diol. The purple permanganate ion is reduced to brown MnO₂, so the purple colour disappears. This is a test for unsaturation.
Why not the others: (B) Ethane would be formed by adding hydrogen, which permanganate cannot do. (C) Alkenes do react; it is alkanes that give no change. (D) An orange colour and a dibromide belong to the bromine-water test.
Key point: Alkene + Baeyer's reagent → diol; purple colour lost.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why must a Grignard reagent, RMgX, be prepared and used in dry ether, with all moisture kept out?
options: A) Water makes the magnesium metal melt
B) Water converts the ether into an alcohol
C) The reagent reacts with water to give the hydrocarbon RH
D) Water oxidises the reagent to a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The reagent reacts with water to give the hydrocarbon RH.
Why: In RMgX the carbon–magnesium bond is strongly polarised, with carbon carrying a partial negative charge, so the alkyl group behaves as a very strong base. It takes a proton from any compound that has one to give, such as water, alcohols or amines: RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X. The reagent is destroyed.
Why not the others: (A) Water does not melt magnesium. (B) Water does not change an ether into an alcohol under these conditions. (D) A carboxylic acid is formed with carbon dioxide followed by acid, not with water.
Key point: Grignard reagent + any source of H⁺ → hydrocarbon.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An unknown alcohol is oxidised gently: the product gives Tollens positive and can be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid. Which alcohol class best fits?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Primary.
Why: Gentle oxidation of a primary alcohol, RCH₂OH, gives an aldehyde, RCHO. An aldehyde reduces Tollens' reagent to a silver mirror and can be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid, RCOOH, with the same number of carbon atoms.
Why not the others: (A) A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the –OH and is not oxidised under gentle conditions. (B) Phenol does not give an aldehyde on oxidation. (C) A secondary alcohol gives a ketone, which does not react with Tollens' reagent and is not easily oxidised further.
Key point: 1° alcohol → aldehyde → acid; 2° alcohol → ketone; 3° alcohol: no reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In Fischer esterification of an acid and alcohol, removing water as it forms increases ester yield at unchanged temperature. Why?
options: A) Removal shifts reversible equilibrium toward ester and water products
B) Water acts as irreversible catalyst only
C) Removal changes the acid into an alkane
D) Alcohol becomes a stronger oxidant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Removal shifts reversible equilibrium toward ester and water products.
Why: Esterification is reversible: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O. By Le Chatelier's principle, removing a product makes the system produce more of it, so more acid and alcohol are converted to ester. The equilibrium constant does not change, because the temperature is the same.
Why not the others: (B) Water is a product, not a catalyst; the catalyst is the mineral acid. (C) No alkane is formed in this reaction. (D) The alcohol acts as a nucleophile, not as an oxidising agent.
Key point: Remove a product to push an equilibrium forward.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Aniline protection and controlled ring substitution
questions.question: The structural sequence shows aniline converted to acetanilide, then predominantly para-bromoacetanilide under controlled bromination, then para-bromoaniline by hydrolysis. Why is acetylation used before bromination?
options: A) To change the amino substituent into a meta director permanently
B) To reduce excessive ring activation while retaining ortho/para direction, then restore NH₂
C) To increase nitrogen donation enough to make tribromination selective for para
D) To replace the amino nitrogen by oxygen before aromatic substitution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To reduce excessive ring activation while retaining ortho/para direction, then restore NH₂.
Why: The –NH₂ group activates the ring so strongly that aniline with bromine gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline at once. In acetanilide the nitrogen lone pair is shared with the C=O group and is less available to the ring. The –NHCOCH₃ group still directs ortho and para but activates much less, and its bulk favours the para position, so one bromine enters. Hydrolysis then gives back the –NH₂ group.
Why not the others: (A) The acetylamino group is still an ortho/para director, and the change is not permanent. (C) Acetylation lowers the donation from nitrogen. (D) Nitrogen stays in the molecule throughout.
Key point: Protect –NH₂ as –NHCOCH₃ to get monosubstitution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A 0.10 m electrolyte solution has freezing depression 0.28 K in a solvent with Kf=1.40 K kg mol⁻¹. What is the observed van't Hoff factor?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(m=0.10\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}\); \(\Delta T_f=0.28\ \mathrm K\); \(K_f=1.40\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta T_f=iK_fm\).
Step 1: Expected depression without dissociation \(=K_fm=1.40\times0.10=0.14\ \mathrm K\).
Worked derivation: \[i=\frac{\Delta T_f}{K_fm}=\frac{0.28}{0.14}=2\]
Why: The observed depression is twice the value for an undissociated solute, so each formula unit gives two particles. The solute behaves as a fully dissociated 1 : 1 electrolyte.
Why not the others: (A) i = 1 would give 0.14 K. (B) i = 1.5 would give 0.21 K. (D) i = 3 would give 0.42 K.
Key point: i = observed colligative property ÷ value calculated for no dissociation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What are the products at the cathode and at the anode?
options: A) Hydrogen at the cathode; chlorine at the anode
B) Sodium at the cathode; oxygen at the anode
C) Chlorine at the cathode; sodium at the anode
D) Sodium at the cathode; chlorine at the anode
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Sodium at the cathode; chlorine at the anode.
Why: Molten sodium chloride contains only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Cations move to the cathode and are reduced: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na. Anions move to the anode and are oxidised: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. No water is present, so hydrogen and oxygen cannot be formed.
Why not the others: (A) Hydrogen is formed at the cathode only when the aqueous solution is electrolysed. (B) Oxygen would need water or hydroxide ions. (C) has the electrodes the wrong way round; reduction takes place at the cathode.
Key point: Molten NaCl: Na and Cl₂. Aqueous NaCl: H₂, Cl₂ and NaOH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Two Arrhenius plots ln k versus 1/T for reactions X and Y are straight; X has slope −6000 K and Y slope −3000 K. If both have the same pre-exponential factor, which has larger activation energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X, twice Y.
Given: Slopes of ln k against 1/T: X, −6000 K; Y, −3000 K.
Formula/Principle: \(\ln k=\ln A-\dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac1T\), so slope \(=-\dfrac{E_a}{R}\).
Step 1: \(E_a(X)=6000R\); \(E_a(Y)=3000R\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{E_a(X)}{E_a(Y)}=\frac{6000R}{3000R}=2\]
Why: A steeper line means the rate constant changes more with temperature, which is the sign of a higher energy barrier. With R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ the values are about 50 and 25 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why not the others: (B) Y has the smaller slope and so the smaller activation energy. (C) Different slopes mean different activation energies. (D) The slope gives the activation energy directly.
Key point: Slope of ln k against 1/T = −E_a/R.
questions.image_alt: Two Arrhenius lines have a common intercept and different negative slopes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A rigid bomb calorimeter is calibrated by supplying 1000 J electrically; its temperature rises by 2.00 K. Combustion of 0.0100 mol of a fuel then raises its temperature by 3.00 K. For the stated combustion reaction, gas mole change is \(\Delta n_g=-1\) per mole fuel. At 300 K, with \(R=8.30\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\), estimate the reaction's molar enthalpy change.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) −152.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Given: Calibration: 1000 J raises T by 2.00 K. Combustion of 0.0100 mol raises T by 3.00 K. \(\Delta n_g=-1\); \(T=300\ \mathrm K\); \(R=8.30\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(C_{\text{cal}}=q/\Delta T\); at constant volume \(q_V=\Delta U\); \(\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT\).
Step 1: \(C_{\text{cal}}=1000/2.00=500\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}\).
Step 2: Heat released \(=500\times3.00=1500\ \mathrm J\) for 0.0100 mol, so \(\Delta U=-1500/0.0100=-150\,000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\).
Step 3: \(\Delta n_gRT=(-1)(8.30)(300)=-2490\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta H=-150\,000-2490=-152\,490\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\approx-152.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: A bomb calorimeter has a fixed volume, so the heat measured is the change in internal energy. At constant pressure the surroundings would also do work on the system, because the number of moles of gas falls; this makes ΔH more negative than ΔU.
Why not the others: (A) −150.0 is ΔU, without the correction. (C) +150.0 has the wrong sign; combustion gives out heat. (D) −147.5 adds the correction with the wrong sign.
Key point: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gRT.
questions.syllabus_anchor: Thermodynamics: calorimetry and measurement of delta U and delta H

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: pH after partial neutralisation of a strong acid
questions.question: 100 mL of 0.10 M HCl is mixed with 100 mL of 0.050 M NaOH. What is the pH of the resulting solution? (log 2.5 = 0.40)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.6.
Given: 100 mL of 0.10 M HCl; 100 mL of 0.050 M NaOH.
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}\); pH from the excess \(\ce{H+}\) in the total volume.
Step 1: \(n(\ce{H+})=0.100\times0.10=0.010\ \mathrm{mol}\); \(n(\ce{OH-})=0.100\times0.050=0.0050\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: Excess \(\ce{H+}=0.010-0.0050=0.0050\ \mathrm{mol}\) in \(0.200\ \mathrm L\).
Step 3: \([\ce{H+}]=0.0050/0.200=0.025\ \mathrm M\).
Worked derivation: \[\mathrm{pH}=-\log(2.5\times10^{-2})=2-0.40=1.6\]
Why: The base neutralises half of the acid. The acid that is left is now in twice the volume, so its concentration is a quarter of the original, not a half.
Why not the others: (A) 1.0 is the pH of the original acid. (B) 1.3 takes [H⁺] as 0.050 M, forgetting that the volume has doubled. (D) 7.0 would need equal moles of acid and base.
Key point: Find the excess moles, then divide by the total volume.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why do transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts in many reactions?
options: A) They have completely filled d orbitals and so do not react
B) They are all gases at room temperature
C) They have very low melting points
D) They can change oxidation state easily and can hold reactant molecules on their surface
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) They can change oxidation state easily and can hold reactant molecules on their surface.
Why: Transition metals have partly filled d orbitals. They can pass between oxidation states, so they form unstable intermediates that open a path of lower activation energy; for example, V₂O₅ in the contact process changes between V(V) and V(IV). As solids they also adsorb reactant molecules, which raises their concentration at the surface and weakens their bonds, as with iron in the Haber process and nickel in hydrogenation.
Why not the others: (A) Their d orbitals are only partly filled, and this is what makes them reactive. (B) They are solids, apart from mercury. (C) Most have high melting points.
Key point: Variable oxidation states + adsorption on the surface = catalytic activity.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Chord endpoints determine two tangents and their intersection
questions.question: A circle centred on the x-axis passes through (0,0) and (6,0). The line x=1 cuts it at P and Q. Tangents at P and Q meet at T. What is the distance OT from the origin?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3/2.
Given: \(\text{circle through }(0,0),\ (6,0),\ \text{centre on the }x\text{-axis};\quad\text{chord }PQ\ \text{on}\ x=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{chord of contact from }T(x_1,y_1)\ \text{to}\ (x-h)^2+y^2=r^2:\ (x_1-h)(x-h)+y_1y=r^2\)
Step 1: \(\text{centre }(3,0),\ r=3:\ (x-3)^2+y^2=9\)
Step 2: \(T=(t,0)\ \text{by symmetry}:\ (t-3)(x-3)=9\)
Step 3: \(x=1:\ (t-3)(-2)=9\Rightarrow t=-\dfrac32\)
Worked derivation: \[OT=\left|-\frac32\right|=\frac32\]
Check: \[CM\cdot CT=2\times\frac92=9=r^2\ \ \left(M=(1,0),\ C=(3,0)\right)\]
Why: \(\text{tangents at the ends of a chord meet on the line through the centre perpendicular to the chord}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac92=CT\) (distance from the centre); (B) \(3=r\); (C) \(6\) (diameter).
Key point: \(CM\cdot CT=r^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: An ellipse centred at origin has foci (±3,0) and directrices x=±25/3. What is its equation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) x²/25+y²/16=1.
Given: \(\text{foci }(\pm3,0),\quad\text{directrices }x=\pm\dfrac{25}{3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(ae=3,\quad\dfrac ae=\dfrac{25}{3},\quad b^2=a^2-a^2e^2\)
Step 1: \(ae\cdot\dfrac ae=a^2=3\times\dfrac{25}{3}=25\)
Step 2: \(b^2=25-9=16\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1\]
Check: \[e=\frac35,\quad\frac ae=\frac{5}{3/5}=\frac{25}{3}\]
Why: \(\text{foci on the }x\text{-axis}\Rightarrow\text{major axis along }x\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{major axis along }y\); (C) \(a^2=9<b^2\); (D) \(b^2=9:\ c^2=16\ne9\).
Key point: \(a^2=(ae)\left(\dfrac ae\right)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the area enclosed by y=4−x² and y=0 between their two x-intercepts.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 32/3.
Given: \(y=4-x^2,\quad y=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\displaystyle\int_{x_1}^{x_2}y\,dx\)
Step 1: \(4-x^2=0\Rightarrow x=\pm2\)
Step 2: \(A=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}(4-x^2)\,dx=2\int_0^2(4-x^2)\,dx\)
Worked derivation: \[A=2\left[4x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=2\left(8-\frac83\right)=\frac{32}{3}\]
Check: \[\tfrac23\times\text{base}\times\text{height}=\tfrac23\times4\times4=\frac{32}{3}\]
Why: \(\text{even integrand}\Rightarrow\text{twice the area from }0\text{ to }2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac{16}{3}\) (one half only); (C) \(8=\tfrac12\times4\times4\) (triangle); (D) \(4\ne\tfrac{32}{3}\).
Key point: \(\text{parabolic segment}=\tfrac23\times\text{enclosing rectangle}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₁ᵉ (ln x)/x dx.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/2.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_1^e\frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(u=\ln x,\quad du=\dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Step 1: \(x=1\Rightarrow u=0;\quad x=e\Rightarrow u=1\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\int_0^1u\,du=\left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac12\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\tfrac12(\ln x)^2\right]=\frac{\ln x}{x}\]
Why: \(\dfrac1x\ \text{is the derivative of}\ \ln x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1=\displaystyle\int_1^e\frac{dx}{x}\); (B) \(\tfrac14\ne\tfrac12\); (D) \(2\) (inverted).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int f(x)f'(x)\,dx=\tfrac12f(x)^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For f(x)=x+9/x on x>0, which interval is f strictly decreasing?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (0,3).
Given: \(f(x)=x+\dfrac9x,\quad x>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(f\ \text{decreasing}\iff f'(x)<0\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=1-\dfrac{9}{x^2}\)
Step 2: \(1-\dfrac{9}{x^2}<0\iff x^2<9\)
Worked derivation: \[0<x<3\]
Check: \[f(1)=10,\ f(2)=6.5,\ f(3)=6,\ f(4)=6.25\]
Why: \(f'(3)=0\ \text{and}\ f'\ \text{changes sign from}\ -\ \text{to}\ +\Rightarrow\text{minimum at }x=3\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x>3:\ f'>0\); (B) \(f'\ \text{changes sign at }3\); (C) \(3<x<9:\ f'>0\).
Key point: \(x+\dfrac{a^2}{x}\ \text{has its minimum}\ 2a\ \text{at}\ x=a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f:(0,∞)→[2,∞) be f(x)=x+1/x. Which classification is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Surjective but not injective.
Given: \(f:(0,\infty)\to[2,\infty),\quad f(x)=x+\dfrac1x\)
Formula/Principle: \(x+\dfrac1x\ge2\ \ (x>0),\ \text{equality at}\ x=1\)
Step 1: \(f(2)=f\left(\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac52\Rightarrow\text{not injective}\)
Step 2: \(y\ge2:\ x^2-yx+1=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{y+\sqrt{y^2-4}}{2}>0\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{range}=[2,\infty)=\text{codomain}\Rightarrow\text{surjective}\]
Check: \[f(x)=f\left(\tfrac1x\right)\ \text{for all}\ x>0\]
Why: \(\text{every value above 2 is taken twice}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(f(2)=f\left(\tfrac12\right)\); (C) \(f(2)=f\left(\tfrac12\right)\); (D) \(\text{range}=[2,\infty)\).
Key point: \(f(x)=f\left(\tfrac1x\right)\Rightarrow\text{not one-one on}\ (0,\infty)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Determinant of a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order
questions.question: A is a real 3×3 skew-symmetric matrix, that is, Aᵀ=−A. What is det A?
options: D) It depends on the entries of A
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.
Given: \(A\in\mathbb R^{3\times3},\quad A^{T}=-A\)
Formula/Principle: \(\det A^{T}=\det A,\quad\det(kA)=k^n\det A\)
Step 1: \(\det A=\det A^{T}=\det(-A)=(-1)^3\det A=-\det A\)
Worked derivation: \[2\det A=0\Rightarrow\det A=0\]
Check: \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\-1&0&3\\-2&-3&0\end{pmatrix}:\ \det A=0-1(0+6)+2(3-0)=0\]
Why: \(n=3\ \text{is odd}\Rightarrow(-1)^n=-1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\det A=-\det A\Rightarrow\det A\ne1\); (C) \(\det A\ne-1\); (D) \(\text{the result holds for every such }A\).
Key point: \(\text{odd-order skew-symmetric matrix}\Rightarrow\det=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Probability of the union of two events
questions.question: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that it is a king or a heart?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4/13.
Given: \(52\ \text{cards};\quad K:\ \text{king};\quad H:\ \text{heart}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(K\cup H)=P(K)+P(H)-P(K\cap H)\)
Step 1: \(P(K)=\dfrac{4}{52},\quad P(H)=\dfrac{13}{52},\quad P(K\cap H)=\dfrac{1}{52}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(K\cup H)=\frac{4+13-1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}\]
Check: \[13\ \text{hearts}+3\ \text{other kings}=16\ \text{cards}\]
Why: \(\text{the king of hearts is counted in both events}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{17}{52}\) (overlap not removed); (B) \(\dfrac14=P(H)\); (D) \(\dfrac1{13}=P(K)\).
Key point: \(\text{subtract the overlap once}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many distinct x in [0,2π) solve cos(3x)=1?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3.
Given: \(\cos3x=1,\quad x\in[0,2\pi)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\cos\theta=1\iff\theta=2n\pi\)
Step 1: \(3x=2n\pi\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{2n\pi}{3}\)
Step 2: \(0\le\dfrac{2n\pi}{3}<2\pi\Rightarrow n=0,1,2\)
Worked derivation: \[x=0,\ \frac{2\pi}{3},\ \frac{4\pi}{3}\ \Rightarrow\ 3\ \text{solutions}\]
Check: \[3x\in[0,6\pi):\ 3x=0,\ 2\pi,\ 4\pi\]
Why: \(\cos3x\ \text{has period}\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\Rightarrow3\ \text{periods in}\ [0,2\pi)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (\(x=0\) omitted); (B) \(4\) (\(x=2\pi\) included); (C) \(6\) (count for \(\cos3x=0\)).
Key point: \(\text{map the interval to the argument, then count}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Parallel-line condition and distance from a plane
questions.question: A line through (1,0,0) has direction vector (1,k,1) and is parallel to the plane \(2x-y+z=5\). What are k and the perpendicular distance between the line and the plane?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3;\ \sqrt6/2\).
Given: \(\text{line}:\ (1,0,0)+t(1,k,1);\quad\text{plane}:\ 2x-y+z=5,\ \mathbf n=(2,-1,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{line}\parallel\text{plane}\iff\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=0;\quad\text{distance}=\dfrac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2-k+1=0\Rightarrow k=3\)
Step 2: \(\text{distance from}\ (1,0,0):\ \dfrac{|2-0+0-5|}{\sqrt{4+1+1}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt6}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{3}{\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\approx1.22\]
Check: \[t=1:\ (2,3,1):\ \frac{|4-3+1-5|}{\sqrt6}=\frac{3}{\sqrt6}\]
Why: \(\text{every point of a line parallel to a plane is at the same distance from it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(3\) (not divided by \(|\mathbf n|\)); (C) \(k=-3:\ \mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=6\ne0\); (D) \(k=1:\ \mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=2\ne0\).
Key point: \(\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n=0\ \text{for a line parallel to a plane}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Points A=(0,1,2), B=(2,3,4), C=(5,6,7) are given. Are they collinear, and what is ratio AB:BC of their segment lengths?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Yes; 2:3.
Given: \(A=(0,1,2),\ B=(2,3,4),\ C=(5,6,7)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{collinear}\iff\overrightarrow{BC}=\lambda\,\overrightarrow{AB}\)
Step 1: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=(2,2,2),\quad\overrightarrow{BC}=(3,3,3)\)
Step 2: \(\overrightarrow{BC}=\tfrac32\,\overrightarrow{AB}\)
Worked derivation: \[AB:BC=2\sqrt3:3\sqrt3=2:3\]
Check: \[\overrightarrow{AC}=(5,5,5)=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}\]
Why: \(\text{parallel vectors with a common point lie on one line}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\overrightarrow{BC}\parallel\overrightarrow{AB}\Rightarrow\text{collinear}\); (C) \(3:2\) (inverted); (D) \(\text{collinear, and}\ AB\ne BC\).
Key point: \(\text{compare direction ratios}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Unequal complex-distance ratio and a circle
questions.question: For \(z=x+iy\), the locus \(\lvert z-1\rvert=2\lvert z+1\rvert\) is a circle. What are its centre and radius?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \((-5/3,0);\ 4/3\).
Given: \(|z-1|=2|z+1|,\quad z=x+iy\)
Formula/Principle: \(|z-a|^2=(x-a)^2+y^2\)
Step 1: \((x-1)^2+y^2=4\left[(x+1)^2+y^2\right]\)
Step 2: \(3x^2+3y^2+10x+3=0\Rightarrow x^2+y^2+\dfrac{10}{3}x+1=0\)
Step 3: \(\left(x+\dfrac53\right)^2+y^2=\dfrac{25}{9}-1=\dfrac{16}{9}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{centre}\left(-\frac53,0\right),\qquad r=\frac43\]
Check: \[z=-\tfrac13:\ \left|-\tfrac43\right|=2\left|\tfrac23\right|;\qquad z=-3:\ |-4|=2|-2|\]
Why: \(\text{ratio of distances from two fixed points}\ne1\Rightarrow\text{circle (Apollonius)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{centre on the wrong side; points are nearer to}\ -1\); (B) \(r^2=\tfrac{16}{9},\ \text{not}\ \tfrac49\); (D) \(|z|=1:\ z=1\ \text{gives}\ 0\ne4\).
Key point: \(\text{square both sides and complete the square}\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Complex numbers: geometric representation; coordinate geometry: circle

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Two roots in distinct strict intervals
questions.question: For which real k does \(f(x)=x^2-2kx+2\) have one root strictly in (0,1) and the other strictly in (2,3)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \((3/2,11/6)\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^2-2kx+2;\quad\text{one root in}\ (0,1),\ \text{the other in}\ (2,3)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{upward parabola}:\ f<0\ \text{strictly between the roots},\ f>0\ \text{outside}\)
Step 1: \(f(0)=2>0\)
Step 2: \(f(1)=3-2k<0\Rightarrow k>\tfrac32\)
Step 3: \(f(2)=6-4k<0\Rightarrow k>\tfrac32\)
Step 4: \(f(3)=11-6k>0\Rightarrow k<\tfrac{11}{6}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac32<k<\frac{11}{6}\]
Check: \[k=1.7:\ x=1.7\pm\sqrt{0.89}=0.757,\ 2.643\]
Why: \(\text{a sign change of }f\text{ on an interval locates exactly one root there}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=\tfrac32:\ f(1)=0\Rightarrow\text{root at }1\notin(0,1)\); (B) \(k=2:\ f(3)=-1<0\); (C) \(k=1:\ f(1)=1>0\).
Key point: \(\text{use the signs of }f\text{ at the interval endpoints}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: In expansion (1+x)⁸, what is the sum of coefficients of x³ and x⁵?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 112.
Given: \((1+x)^8\)
Formula/Principle: \([x^r]=\dbinom8r,\quad\dbinom8r=\dbinom8{8-r}\)
Step 1: \(\dbinom83=56,\quad\dbinom85=\dbinom83=56\)
Worked derivation: \[56+56=112\]
Check: \[\binom83=\frac{8\cdot7\cdot6}{6}=56\]
Why: \(\text{binomial coefficients are symmetric}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(56\) (one coefficient); (C) \(70=\dbinom84\); (D) \(28=\dbinom82\).
Key point: \(\dbinom nr=\dbinom n{n-r}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Three arithmetic means are inserted between 4 and 16 to form a five-term arithmetic progression. What is the sum of the three inserted means?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 30.
Given: \(4,\ A_1,\ A_2,\ A_3,\ 16\ \text{in AP}\)
Formula/Principle: \(d=\dfrac{b-a}{n+1}\)
Step 1: \(d=\dfrac{16-4}{4}=3\)
Step 2: \(A_1,A_2,A_3=7,\ 10,\ 13\)
Worked derivation: \[7+10+13=30\]
Check: \[n\cdot\frac{a+b}{2}=3\times10=30\]
Why: \(\text{sum of }n\text{ arithmetic means}=n\times\text{the single arithmetic mean}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(20=4+16\); (C) \(40\ne30\); (D) \(60\ne30\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum A_i=n\,\frac{a+b}{2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.question: Two cars start together at x=0. A travels at constant +12 m s⁻¹ and B starts from rest with acceleration +3 m s⁻². When do they next have the same position?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8 s.
Given: \(x_A=12t;\quad x_B=\tfrac12(3)t^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(x_A=x_B\)
Step 1: \(12t=1.5t^2\Rightarrow t(1.5t-12)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[t=8\ \mathrm s\ \ (t\ne0)\]
Check: \[x_A=96\ \mathrm m,\quad x_B=1.5\times64=96\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(\text{B is slower at first, then faster}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4\ \mathrm s:\ v_B=v_A\ (\text{equal speeds, maximum separation})\); (B) \(6\ \mathrm s:\ 72\ne54\); (D) \(12\ \mathrm s:\ 144\ne216\).
Key point: \(\text{equal positions, not equal velocities}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Dimensional analysis of the period of a pendulum
questions.question: The period T of a simple pendulum is assumed to depend on its length l and on the acceleration due to gravity g as T=k lᵃ gᵇ, where k is a dimensionless constant. What are a and b?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2 and −1/2.
Given: \(T=k\,l^ag^b,\quad[T]=\mathrm T,\ [l]=\mathrm L,\ [g]=\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{dimensions on both sides must be equal}\)
Step 1: \(\mathrm T^1=\mathrm L^a\left(\mathrm{L\,T^{-2}}\right)^b=\mathrm L^{a+b}\,\mathrm T^{-2b}\)
Step 2: \(\mathrm T:\ -2b=1\Rightarrow b=-\tfrac12\)
Step 3: \(\mathrm L:\ a+b=0\Rightarrow a=\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[T=k\sqrt{\frac lg}\]
Check: \[\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm m}{\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}}}=\mathrm s\]
Why: \(\text{mass does not appear}\Rightarrow T\ \text{is independent of the mass of the bob}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac lg:\ \mathrm{T^2}\); (B) \(\sqrt{\dfrac gl}:\ \mathrm{T^{-1}}\); (C) \(\sqrt{lg}:\ \mathrm{L\,T^{-1}}\).
Key point: \(\text{equate the powers of each base dimension}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An open tank of water accelerates horizontally to the right with acceleration a. The diagram specifies the tank axes and acceleration but not the final water surface. In the tank frame, which side is higher at equilibrium, and what is the tangent of the surface's angle to the horizontal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Left; a/g.
Given: \(\text{tank accelerates to the right with }a\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{tank frame}:\ \mathbf g_{\text{eff}}=\mathbf g-\mathbf a;\quad\text{free surface}\perp\mathbf g_{\text{eff}}\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf g_{\text{eff}}=(-a,\ -g)\ \ (\text{backward and downward})\)
Step 2: \(\text{surface}\perp\mathbf g_{\text{eff}}\Rightarrow\text{slope}=-\dfrac ag\)
Worked derivation: \[\tan\theta=\frac ag,\qquad\text{left (rear) side higher}\]
Check: \[\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}=-\rho a<0\Rightarrow\text{pressure, and so depth, greater at the rear}\]
Why: \(\text{a net force to the right on each layer needs higher pressure on its left}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{right side higher gives a force to the left}\); (C) \(a\to0:\ \dfrac ga\to\infty\ \text{(vertical surface)}\); (D) \(\text{both errors}\).
Key point: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac ag\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: A uniform disc has mass M and radius R. What is its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane through a point on its rim?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 3MR²/2.
Given: \(\text{uniform disc},\ M,\ R;\quad\text{axis}\perp\text{plane through a point on the rim}\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=I_{\text{cm}}+Md^2,\quad I_{\text{cm}}=\tfrac12MR^2\)
Step 1: \(d=R\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\tfrac12MR^2+MR^2=\tfrac32MR^2\]
Check: \[I>I_{\text{cm}}\]
Why: \(\text{the axis through the centre of mass gives the least moment of inertia among parallel axes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12MR^2=I_{\text{cm}}\); (C) \(\tfrac54MR^2\) (tangent in the plane of the disc); (D) \(2MR^2\) (ring about a point on its rim).
Key point: \(I=I_{\text{cm}}+Md^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Cascaded cyclic heat-engine balances with an external load
questions.question: A cyclic heat engine absorbs 800 J per cycle and converts 40% of it to shaft work. All its rejected heat feeds a second cyclic engine of efficiency 1/3. A parasitic external load consumes 40 J from the combined shaft output per cycle, without returning heat to either engine. What are the useful efficiency relative to the original 800 J input and the heat rejected by the second engine?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 55%; 320 J.
Given: \(Q_1=800\ \mathrm J,\ \eta_1=0.40;\quad\eta_2=\tfrac13;\quad\text{load}=40\ \mathrm J\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\eta Q_{\text{in}},\quad Q_{\text{out}}=Q_{\text{in}}-W\)
Step 1: \(W_1=0.40\times800=320\ \mathrm J,\quad Q_{\text{out},1}=480\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(W_2=\tfrac13\times480=160\ \mathrm J,\quad Q_{\text{out},2}=320\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(W_{\text{useful}}=320+160-40=440\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\eta=\frac{440}{800}=0.55=55\%;\qquad Q_{\text{out},2}=320\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[800=440+40+320\]
Why: \(\text{energy is conserved in each cycle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(60\%=\dfrac{480}{800}\) (load not subtracted); (B) \(480\ \mathrm J=Q_{\text{out},1}\); (D) \(40\%=\eta_1\ \text{alone}\).
Key point: \(\eta_{\text{combined}}=\eta_1+(1-\eta_1)\eta_2\ \text{before the load}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two springs of constants k and 3k support a mass m in parallel. What is oscillation period divided by period with spring k alone?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: \(k_1=k,\ k_2=3k\ \text{in parallel},\ \text{mass }m\)
Formula/Principle: \(k_{\text{parallel}}=k_1+k_2,\quad T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk}\)
Step 1: \(k_{\text{eff}}=4k\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{T'}{T}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{4k}}=\frac12\]
Check: \[\text{stiffer support}\Rightarrow\text{shorter period}\]
Why: \(\text{parallel springs share the same extension}\Rightarrow\text{forces add}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (inverted); (C) \(\tfrac14\) (root not taken); (D) \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) (series: \(k_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac34k\), inverted).
Key point: \(T\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt k}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two coherent sources have equal amplitudes and a fixed initial phase difference π at a screen point where their path lengths are equal. What intensity relative to the one-source intensity I₀ results there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.
Given: \(a_1=a_2=a,\quad\text{source phase difference}=\pi,\quad\text{path difference}=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=I_1+I_2+2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(\phi=\pi+0=\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[I=I_0+I_0+2I_0\cos\pi=0\]
Check: \[A=a+a\cos\pi=0\]
Why: \(\text{total phase difference}=\text{source phase difference}+\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\text{path difference}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4I_0\) (\(\phi=0\)); (B) \(2I_0\) (incoherent sum); (D) \(I_0\) (one source only).
Key point: \(\phi=\pi\Rightarrow\text{destructive interference}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.sub_topic: Potential and field inside a charged spherical shell
questions.question: A thin conducting spherical shell of radius R carries charge Q. Taking the potential at infinity as zero and k=1/4πε₀, what are the potential and the electric field at its centre?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) kQ/R and 0.
Given: \(\text{thin conducting shell},\ R,\ Q;\quad V(\infty)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Gauss's law};\quad V(r)=-\displaystyle\int_\infty^rE\,dr\)
Step 1: \(r<R:\ q_{\text{enclosed}}=0\Rightarrow E=0\)
Step 2: \(r\ge R:\ E=\dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\Rightarrow V(R)=\dfrac{kQ}{R}\)
Worked derivation: \[E(0)=0;\qquad V(0)=V(R)=\frac{kQ}{R}\]
Check: \[E=-\frac{dV}{dr}=0\ \text{inside}\Rightarrow V\ \text{constant inside}\]
Why: \(\text{zero field means constant potential, not zero potential}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(V(0)=\dfrac{kQ}{R}\ne0\); (B) \(E(0)=0\ne\dfrac{kQ}{R^2}\); (C) \(E(0)=0\).
Key point: \(\text{inside a charged shell}:\ E=0,\ V=\dfrac{kQ}{R}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Cells in series with internal resistance
questions.question: Two cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω, are joined in series and connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor. What current flows?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.0 A.
Given: \(\varepsilon=1.5\ \mathrm V,\ r=0.5\ \Omega\ \text{each};\quad\text{two in series};\quad R=2.0\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=\dfrac{n\varepsilon}{R+nr}\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon_{\text{total}}=3.0\ \mathrm V,\quad r_{\text{total}}=1.0\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{3.0}{2.0+1.0}=1.0\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[V_R=IR=2.0\ \mathrm V;\quad\text{each cell}:\ 1.5-1.0\times0.5=1.0\ \mathrm V\]
Why: \(\text{series}:\ \text{emfs add and internal resistances add}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac{3.0}{2.0}=1.5\ \mathrm A\) (internal resistance omitted); (C) \(\dfrac{1.5}{2.5}=0.6\ \mathrm A\) (one cell only); (D) \(\dfrac{3.0}{1.0}=3.0\ \mathrm A\) (\(R\) omitted).
Key point: \(I=\dfrac{n\varepsilon}{R+nr}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Equal activities and separate parent decay populations
questions.question: A closed sample initially contains 900 radioactive parent atoms of types P and Q in total, with equal initial activities. Their half-lives are 2 h and 4 h. Each parent produces one stable daughter, initially absent. What is the expected total number of daughter atoms after 4 h?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 525.
Given: \(N_P+N_Q=900;\quad\text{equal initial activities};\quad T_P=2\ \mathrm h,\ T_Q=4\ \mathrm h;\quad t=4\ \mathrm h\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\lambda N=\dfrac{\ln2}{T}N,\quad N(t)=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{N_P}{2}=\dfrac{N_Q}{4}\Rightarrow N_Q=2N_P\Rightarrow N_P=300,\ N_Q=600\)
Step 2: \(N_P(4)=300\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=75,\quad N_Q(4)=600\left(\tfrac12\right)^1=300\)
Step 3: \(\text{decayed}:\ 225+300\)
Worked derivation: \[N_{\text{daughter}}=525\]
Check: \[75+300+525=900\]
Why: \(\text{equal activity with a longer half-life needs more atoms}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(375=75+300\) (parents left); (B) \(450\) (half of the total); (C) \(600=N_Q(0)\).
Key point: \(\text{equal activities}\Rightarrow\dfrac{N_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{N_2}{T_2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two coaxial loops have defined positive normal toward the observer. Current in primary rises and its field through secondary points toward observer. What induced field direction does secondary current create?
options: B) Away from observer, opposing increasing flux
C) Zero because loops do not touch
D) Alternates instantaneously with no change in primary direction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Away from observer, opposing increasing flux.
Given: \(\text{primary field through the secondary}:\ \text{towards the observer, increasing}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon_2=-\dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt}>0\ \ (\text{towards the observer})\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf B_{\text{induced}}\ \text{points away from the observer}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{secondary current clockwise as seen by the observer}\]
Check: \[\text{aiding the change}\Rightarrow\text{flux grows without limit (energy not conserved)}\]
Why: \(\text{Lenz's law}:\ \text{the induced current opposes the change in flux}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{aiding the increase violates Lenz's law}\); (C) \(\text{flux linkage needs no contact}\); (D) \(\dfrac{d\Phi_2}{dt}\ \text{keeps one sign while the current rises}\).
Key point: \(\text{rising flux}\Rightarrow\text{induced field opposite to it}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A ray goes from glass n=1.5 into air n=1.0 at incidence angle 50° measured to normal. What happens at the interface?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Total internal reflection.
Given: \(n_1=1.5,\quad n_2=1.0,\quad i=50^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\theta_c=\dfrac{1.0}{1.5}=0.667\Rightarrow\theta_c=41.8^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\sin50^\circ=0.766>0.667\)
Worked derivation: \[i=50^\circ>\theta_c=41.8^\circ\Rightarrow\text{total internal reflection}\]
Check: \[n_1\sin i=1.5\times0.766=1.15>1\Rightarrow\text{no real angle of refraction}\]
Why: \(\text{denser to rarer medium, beyond the critical angle}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(1.5\sin50^\circ\ne1.0\sin50^\circ\); (C) \(1.0\sin30^\circ=0.5\ne1.15\); (D) \(\text{clear glass does not absorb the light}\).
Key point: \(\text{TIR when}\ n_1\sin i>n_2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Phase and power in a purely capacitive circuit
questions.question: An alternating voltage is applied across an ideal capacitor. How is the current related in phase to the voltage, and what is the average power consumed over a cycle?
options: A) The current lags the voltage by π/2; the power is V_rms I_rms
B) The current leads the voltage by π/2; the average power is zero
C) The current is in phase with the voltage; the average power is zero
D) The current leads the voltage by π; the power is V_rms I_rms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The current leads the voltage by π/2; the average power is zero.
Given: \(v=V_0\sin\omega t\ \text{across an ideal capacitor }C\)
Formula/Principle: \(q=Cv,\quad i=\dfrac{dq}{dt},\quad\bar P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(i=\omega CV_0\cos\omega t=\omega CV_0\sin\left(\omega t+\tfrac\pi2\right)\)
Step 2: \(\phi=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow\cos\phi=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\bar P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\frac\pi2=0\]
Check: \[p=vi=\tfrac12\omega CV_0^2\sin2\omega t\ \Rightarrow\ \text{average over a cycle}=0\]
Why: \(\text{energy stored in one quarter-cycle is returned in the next}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{lagging by}\ \tfrac\pi2\ \text{is the inductor}\); (C) \(\text{in phase is the resistor, with}\ \bar P\ne0\); (D) \(\phi=\tfrac\pi2,\ \text{not}\ \pi\).
Key point: \(\text{capacitor: current leads; inductor: current lags; both wattless}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A half-wave rectifier fed by v(t)=V₀sinωt drives resistance R with ideal diode. What is average output power over a full cycle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) V₀²/(4R).
Given: \(v=V_0\sin\omega t,\quad\text{ideal diode},\ R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar P=\dfrac1T\displaystyle\int_0^T\frac{v_{\text{out}}^2}{R}\,dt\)
Step 1: \(v_{\text{out}}=V_0\sin\omega t\ \left(0<t<\tfrac T2\right),\quad v_{\text{out}}=0\ \left(\tfrac T2<t<T\right)\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac1T\displaystyle\int_0^{T/2}\sin^2\omega t\,dt=\dfrac14\)
Worked derivation: \[\bar P=\frac{V_0^2}{R}\cdot\frac14=\frac{V_0^2}{4R}\]
Check: \[\text{full sine wave}:\ \frac{V_0^2}{2R};\ \text{half the cycle removed}\Rightarrow\frac{V_0^2}{4R}\]
Why: \(\text{the diode conducts for one half-cycle only}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{V_0^2}{R}\) (peak power); (B) \(\dfrac{V_0^2}{2R}\) (no rectification); (D) \(\dfrac{V_0^2}{8R}\) (halved twice).
Key point: \(V_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{V_0}{2}\ \text{for a half-wave rectified output}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fringe spacing and tracked phase-sheet displacement
questions.question: In a Young setup the original fringe width is \(\beta=\lambda D/d\). The slit separation is changed to 2d, and a thin sheet of refractive index 1.50 is placed at one slit. The tracked bright fringe with zero total optical path difference shifts by \(3\beta/4\) from the geometric axis. In the paraxial approximation, what are the new fringe width and sheet thickness?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\beta/2;\ 3\lambda\).
Given: \(\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d};\quad d\to2d;\quad\mu=1.50;\quad\text{shift}=\dfrac{3\beta}{4}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\beta'=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d'},\quad\text{shift}=\dfrac{(\mu-1)tD}{d'}\)
Step 1: \(\beta'=\dfrac{\lambda D}{2d}=\dfrac\beta2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{(1.50-1)\,tD}{2d}=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{t}{4}=\dfrac{3\lambda}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[t=3\lambda\]
Check: \[(\mu-1)t=1.5\lambda\Rightarrow\text{shift}=1.5\ \text{new fringes}=1.5\times\frac\beta2=\frac{3\beta}{4}\]
Why: \(\text{the sheet adds optical path}\ (\mu-1)t\ \text{at one slit}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\beta\) (\(\beta\propto d\)); (B) \(t=\tfrac32\lambda:\ \text{shift}=0.75\times\dfrac\beta2=\dfrac{3\beta}{8}\); (C) \(t=6\lambda:\ \text{shift}=3\times\dfrac\beta2=\dfrac{3\beta}{2}\).
Key point: \(\text{number of fringes shifted}=\dfrac{(\mu-1)t}{\lambda}\)
